transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Desai (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Opal ML Lead), Carlos Vega (Opal CTO), Ellen Park (Opal PM), Tom Hargrove (Opal SRE)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC sync focused on recent quality regressions observed in the pilot, discussion of scoring adjustments, triage plan for 12 failing prompt variants, and guardrail tightening. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- Regression bisection plan
- Scoring rubric changes (precision-weighted)
- Guardrail rule hardening and false-positive reduction
- Latency vs cost for hosted vs dedicated routing
- Security docs & network constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. we're on for forty six minutes. quick agenda recap: regressions, scoring rubric, guardrails, and next steps. Ravi and I will run through the failing examples then hand to Priya for context.
[00:24] Priya Singh: yeah thanks Maya. we saw a spike in false positives on Friday after the small model swap, about 12 prompts that moved from pass to fail on the scorecard. some are subtle, like entity hallucination, others are tone/regulatory misses.
[00:47] Ravi Desai: okay I pulled the run logs — so we've got the version matrix here. looks like the lower-quantized variant we tested had higher hallucination on long-context prompts. might be KV cache mismatch, or kv cash — excuse me — cache warmup behaving oddly.
[01:12] Carlos Vega: is this the variant that's running in hosted or dedicated? i thought we had dedicated routes for the heavy batch.
[01:24] Maya Chen: currently it's routed to hosted by default for the trial burst, but we did the quick fallback to the 8-bit variant. we can reproduce both hosted and dedicated in the bench.
[01:37] Tom Hargrove: from our side, network egress is still a concern. if you want us to run dedicated in our VPC we need a peering window, maybe the weekend.
[01:50] Ravi Desai: noted. in terms of quality, i've run a quick delta on the scoring components: semantic accuracy, hallucination penalty, regulatory flag, and style. the failing 12 mostly score low on hallucination penalty and regulatory.
[02:15] Ellen Park: what are we using for the scoring thresholds? i remember we had a 0.7 pass cutoff?
[02:25] Maya Chen: yeah base pass is 0.7. Priya suggested moving to a precision-weighted rubric to avoid reward for noisy recall. that means higher weight on precision and regulatory flags.
[02:40] Priya Singh: yep, for our use case false positives are more harmful than misses. e.g. a mistaken instruction that bypasses compliance is critical. so we prefer conservatism.
[02:58] Ravi Desai: practically speaking, we can change the weights and rerun the scoreboard. also short-term we can add guardrail rules in the rule editor to catch the specific failure modes — phrase-level denies and entity buckets.
[03:20] Maya Chen: can you talk through the guardrail rules you'd add, Ravi?
[03:28] Ravi Desai: sure. first we add a deny rule with high priority for pattern matches that correlate to hallucination of regulated entities, second a thresholded classifier that pushes to safe-fallback if classifier confidence < 0.6, third a paraphrase check to detect overconfident rewrites.
[03:50] Carlos Vega: that paraphrase check sounds compute-heavy. will it add latency? our SLO is 450ms p95.
[04:02] Ravi Desai: good question. the paraphrase check can be run asynchronously in the pipeline or as a fast shallow similarity hash. we also have a staged path: run light-weight checks inline, heavier checks async to the sidecar with an immediate safe fallback option.
[04:26] Tom Hargrove: how does that affect tokens and billing for us? if there's an async check it might double tokens in worst-case.
[04:36] Maya Chen: true — we can model cost versus false-positive reduction. Redwood Optimize suggested batching and cache tweaks already reduced token spend by ~12% in similar pilots. we'll send a cost projection.
[04:55] Priya Singh: on the regression bisection, can you briefly describe the approach? we want to minimize manual labeling.
[05:05] Ravi Desai: sure. we run a binary bisection on prompt variants: isolate smallest subset that flips the pass/fail. basically we run A/B across checkpoints and prompt mutations, then run statistical significance checks to find the suspect commit or prompt change. it's automated but we still need human validation for the final suspected prompts.
[05:34] Ellen Park: how many tests do you think this will generate? we have limited annotation bandwidth.
[05:41] Ravi Desai: the bisection will produce roughly 25-40 suspect prompts to validate for the 12 failing cases, but we aim to reduce to top 12-15 that likely caused the shift.
[05:57] Carlos Vega: do we need to give you more data or examples? Priya can annotate but it's a lot of work.
[06:06] Priya Singh: i can sample some from the failure bucket and mark hard negatives. i'll aim to give two each for now.
[06:14] Maya Chen: perfect. action item for Priya to upload annotations to the shared secure folder. maya will share link.
[06:23] Ravi Desai: also, for the scoring rubric change: switching to precision-weighted means the score distribution will shift. we should agree on new pass threshold after we simulate it on last week's dataset.
[06:40] Priya Singh: simulation is fine, but i'd expect threshold to go up to 0.75 once we up-weight precision.
[06:48] Maya Chen: let's run the sim and reconvene.
[07:00] (short pause, background typing)
[07:15] Carlos Vega: one thing on guardrails — we saw false positives where the rule engine flagged benign content due to fuzzy matching. we need to tune to avoid blocking correct answers.
[07:28] Ravi Desai: absolutely — there is a tradeoff. we can use a layered approach: strict deny rules for high-risk patterns and lower-priority fuzzy rules that add a human review or soft-fallback.
[07:45] Ellen Park: can Redwood provide a sample ruleset tuned for telecom/networks compliance? we have specific regulatory wording.
[07:54] Maya Chen: yes, we'll share a telecom-oriented starter pack. we'll also include the mapping between our rule priority and the scorecard impact.
[08:07] Tom Hargrove: security side note — we'll need SOC2 docs and encryption details; we also need to understand KMS/HSM options if we go private.
[08:19] Maya Chen: i'll put SOC2 and on-prem checklist in the secure share. we support KMS integration and customer-managed HSM for Private.
[08:30] Priya Singh: great. also, for privacy, do you log user PII in the inference logs? we need that info for compliance.
[08:39] Ravi Desai: logs can be configured to redact or not capture user content. for Private deployments we can disable content logging entirely and forward only metadata.
[08:51] Carlos Vega: okay thanks.
[08:57] Maya Chen: quick demo time: ravi, can you pull up the failing example 7?
[09:04] Ravi Desai: sure pulling... (mouse click noises) 
[09:20] Ravi Desai: Example 7: prompt asks for router configuration snippets under a regulatory constraint; model inserted a made-up certificate ID, that's the hallucination. here's current output and the expected safe response.
[09:38] Priya Singh: yes that's the one. the made-up certificate is dangerous. nice repro.
[09:45] Ravi Desai: we can add pattern-checking for cert formats and deny generation when a generated identifier doesn't match known registry prefixes.
[09:58] Carlos Vega: how do you validate registry prefixes at runtime without leaking our internal registry?
[10:06] Ravi Desai: you can provide a hashed allowlist or run the check on-prem. we also have an option to consult a stored tokenized set via VPC-only lookup.
[10:18] Tom Hargrove: that VPC-only lookup is preferable. we'll need offline sync windows for allowance updates.
[10:27] Maya Chen: noted. we'll surface the sync pattern in the ops doc.
[10:34] (timestamp jump — 10:34 to 14:02, brief offline chat)
[14:02] Maya Chen: back on. next big item: cost/latency tradeoffs. Ravi, you ran host vs dedicated bench?
[14:12] Ravi Desai: yes. on our small sample, dedicated gives p95 improvement from 480ms to 360ms for the large-context path, but cost per token increases ~18% without batching. with batching and prefix caching, cost gap narrows to ~6%.
[14:32] Carlos Vega: 360ms p95 is good. our SLA target is 400ms for critical flows. 360 would be safe. what infra is that on? A100s?
[14:41] Ravi Desai: that's on T4x2 equivalent for dedicated; if you choose higher tier GPUs latency can be even lower. hosted used mixed instances.
[14:53] Priya Singh: any change in quality between hosted and dedicated? noise from quantization aside, we saw the same flips tied to the model variant not the routing.
[15:03] Ravi Desai: correct. routing didn't change the model internals. it's the model variant and tokenization. dedicated can pin to the float16 variant consistently.
[15:15] Ellen Park: how long to spin up dedicated for a pilot? we need it for a 2-week stress window.
[15:22] Maya Chen: for pilot customers we can provision dedicated pools in 72 hours once the contract is signed and region is available. there's also burst capacity if needed.
[15:33] Carlos Vega: contract — what's the minimum commitment?
[15:37] Maya Chen: we can do a short pilot commit of one month at lower reserved capacity, or a month-to-month flexible reserved; we'll follow up with pricing.
[15:47] Tom Hargrove: re: bench results, can you provide raw traces? our infra team wants to run flamegraph on the path.
[15:55] Ravi Desai: yes we'll share trace samples stripped of PII.
[16:05] Priya Singh: switching back to guardrails — for the 12 failing prompts, can you list which are pattern vs model-flip?
[16:14] Ravi Desai: preliminarily six pattern-match hallucinations, four model-flips tied to quantization, two are prompt-sensitivity where minor phrasing changed the intent.
[16:26] Maya Chen: so action is bisection for the quantization and prompt normalization for the sensitivity cases.
[16:33] Priya Singh: for prompt normalization, can Redwood run augmentation tests to find robust phrasings?
[16:40] Ravi Desai: yes we have a prompt-augmentation harness. we'll generate paraphrases and test stability score.
[16:49] Carlos Vega: do we have automated metrics to detect emergent hallucination over time? like a rolling-window alert?
[16:57] Maya Chen: Redwood Console supports threshold alerts on scorecard drift, and we can tie those to automated rollbacks or canaries.
[17:08] Tom Hargrove: what about eval frequency? daily, hourly?
[17:12] Priya Singh: for our use case daily is okay for early pilot, hourly might be overkill.
[17:18] Ravi Desai: we'll set daily aggregation with an option for per-route sampling at higher frequency for risky flows.
[17:28] (brief cross-talk)
[17:35] Carlos Vega: on benchmarking, can Redwood run a side-by-side that matches our traffic profile? we have lots of long multi-turn contexts.
[17:45] Ravi Desai: yes we'll use your anonymized traffic replay to populate the bench and show p95/p50/p99 and token spend.
[17:55] Ellen Park: timeline for the regression bisection and the simulation of new rubric?
[18:00] Maya Chen: we proposed bisection by 2026-03-23 and rubric sim by 2026-03-25.
[18:08] Priya Singh: thumbs up.
[18:12] Maya Chen: any blockers from Opal?
[18:15] Tom Hargrove: only the VPC peering schedule — i'll confirm the weekend window by Friday.
[18:23] Carlos Vega: and we need the pricing sheet.
[18:26] Maya Chen: will send pricing and detailed bench spreadsheet.
[18:31] Priya Singh: one more question on false positives: is it possible to add a human-in-the-loop for the flagged cases with high business impact?
[18:39] Ravi Desai: yes, Redwood supports soft-fail hooks to create review tasks and route to your internal queue or a human review UI.
[18:48] Ellen Park: good to know.
[18:52] Maya Chen: ok let's recap next steps. we'll put them in the shared doc. ravi any final notes?
[19:00] Ravi Desai: just that i'll start the bisection run now and send the reduced test set. also we'll demo the rule edits in the next call.
[19:09] Maya Chen: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the secure links and SOC2. meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
